bottleneck: Precise gene correction via homology-directed repair (HDR) competes with error-prone non-homologous end joining, which dominates in most mammalian cells, especially non-dividing ones. HDR templates are inefficiently delivered and rarely used by the cell, so most edits become random indels instead of exact corrections. Inhibiting NHEJ in vivo is not yet a safe or practical strategy.
current_state: Cell-cycle synchronization and small-molecule HDR boosters work in vitro but translate poorly in vivo. Most therapeutic edits therefore rely on gene disruption rather than precise correction.

title: HDR loses to NHEJ, blocking precise in vivo correction
why_it_blocks: True cures require rewriting mutations exactly, not just breaking genes. As long as HDR loses, the edit that medicine needs most stays the hardest to deliver, limiting CRISPR to knockout-style therapies.
